newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany, France say key EMU issues resolved.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France say key EMU issues resolved.

text.p: Germany and France said on Tuesday they had resolved all major differences over the creation of a stable European currency and were more confident than ever that the Euro would be launched in 1999.

Speaking after a regular meeting of the Franco-German economic council, which groups the top financial officials of the two countries, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said: "We have reached very broad agreement on decisive issues."
"We are much further than I expected a year ago," he added in remarks at a news conference.

The finance ministers and central bank governors of the two countries at the heart of Europe's single currency plans came to the Bavarian town of Kempten with two key agenda points -- an exchange of view on their economies and preparation for a meeting of European finance officials in Dublin this weekend.
Talks in Kempten began with some delay after bad weather diverted the officials aircraft to Stuttgart. They arrived in Kempten mid-morning after starting talks in the airport lounge.

The meeting fell at a critical time for the two countries' domestically -- sandwiched between the approval of a key package of German spending cuts, approved last Friday, and a vote on a controversial budget in the French parliament.

Speaking just one day ahead the Paris budget talks, Waigel told reporters that both countries intended to rein in their budget deficits to a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product, the limit set in the Maastricht Treaty.
The two countries also gave a bullish outlook for economic growth and trumpeted measures aimed at reducing joblessness.
The Maastricht Treaty requires countries which wish to enter EMU to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget decifits and public borrowing.
Optimistic that they will both go to the Dublin meeting with the backing of fiscal strength, the powerful Franco-German axis also laid out its view of how talks there should proceed.

The Dublin meeting will discuss still unresolved issues of how to maintain fiscal discipline once monetary union starts, what to do with currencies which do not pass the entry test to join the Euro, and the legal framework for the currency's use.

Oozing with confidence that their position would find favour with other EU financial leaders, Waigel and his French counterpart Jean Arthuis said the two countries believed their plans would create the basis for a stable European currency.

"We are agreed that long-term budgetary discipline is seen as indispensible by both Germany and France if the stability of the Euro is to be guaranteed," Arthuis told reporters, echoing almost word for word a statement from Waigel.

Separately German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in a speech in Buenos Aires that Maastricht entry criteria should not be changed and predicted that EMU would start with five to seven European Union members.
